# Pavol's decisions since 2026-09-16, judged against the designers' intent

## In short

- On every large call he has gone the way the designers' own implementers went: one library, the exclusion rule kept and the number tower flattened, sizes in the types with unboxed storage, the 2009 overload sentence dropped, `comprises` read at the level of values, conversions never changing which declaration runs. Each of these is what the type group built or wrote last, not what the early draft wished.
- Where the designers left no word, his calls are pragmatic, consistent with each other, and mostly in the library's own patterns. Two are not: row 330 (`floor` on a float returning an unbounded integer), decided on a premise route A then removed and against the library's consistent declaration; and the written `extends Object` bound of batch 7, which turned a compile-time refusal into a JVM crash the switch-over will meet (row 447).
- No cardinal error of commission. Row 330 has cost nothing yet and reverses for the price of one entry. Row 447 costs one code-generator rung and must land before the switch-over.
- The errors of omission are in the plan, not in the decisions: the switch-over (phase 4) is the largest and least designed piece; phase 5's collision between "no model line changes" and "sizes in the model's own types" is measured (decision D's diff: 21 lines out, 29 in) but not yet faced by him; the unboxed store's mechanism (decision A) has no design and the "fast" half of the goal rests on it.
- The standard itself has two voices on the tower, and his decisions follow the later one. The record's own brief for route A did not cite the sentence that most supports it (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:501-502`).
- He has not gone astray. Section 6 lists eleven things to decide or confirm, the first four before batch 7b.

## 1. Primer: what the designers were aiming for

Terms are defined where they first appear. "The team" is the Sun/Oracle Fortress group, 2003-2012. "Walk" is the interpreter; "the checker" is the static type checker, which runs only on the compiled path. "The one library" is the interpreter's library (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`), which his decision of 2026-09-21 makes the library the compiler checks. "The prelude" is the compiler's own smaller library (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`), to be deleted at "the switch-over", the day the compiled path reads the one library.

### The three texts, and which is the designers' latest word

- The 2008 release is `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`, 262 pages, the team's own artefact (`403afbe0b`, 2008-03-31).
- The Working Draft is the LaTeX under `Specification/`. The team's last edit to its text is 2010-12-09 (`44e03b176`). Steele cloned it whole into `Specification-1.0-frozen/` on 2012-01-04, so the frozen directory is byte for byte the draft of 2011-02-02, not the 1.0 text; only the PDF beside it is 1.0 (`coordinator/spec-lineage.md` §§ 1-2, checked). "July 2012" on the revival's PDF is the date of a parentless import commit, chosen by the revival (`414b790e3`), not of any edit.
- The restart is `Documentation/Specification/`, begun 2012-02-20 by Luchangco, abandoned 2012-05-31 with most chapters empty. Its Types chapter (`Prose/Language/types.tick`, 1,056 lines) is fresh 2012 prose and the team's last word on types, exclusion and `comprises`. It has no chapter on static parameters, numbers, coercion beyond a relation, or the library.
- The papers: the OOPSLA 2011 type-system paper (`Papers/Types/`), Naden's 2012 journal text on the return-type rule (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`, last touched 2012-08-31, the project's last day), the Welterweight calculus (2012), the four patents filed 2012-08-31, and Steele's 2016 retrospective (`research/extracts/SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md`).
- So "the designers' latest word" is not one text. On types and the exclusion rule it is the 2012 Types chapter and Naden. On the library, static parameters, coercion, overloading resolution and the number chapters it is the Working Draft, whose text on those topics is 2008-2010. On what they actually made run, it is the code: the interpreter's library (2007-2012, never type-checked) and the compiler's prelude and checker (2009-2012).

### Numbers and the tower

- A **tower** is a chain of number types where each is a subtype of the next: an integer is a rational is a real. In the interpreter's library the team built exactly that in 2008: `ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: AnyIntegral <: QQ <: RR64 <: Number`, and kept it to the end (`reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md` § 7, commits `cfe16b43b`, `fca589bbb`). The library chapters of the Working Draft say the same in prose: ℤ "is a subtype of ℚ" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex:28-29`) and the listing has `trait ℤ extends { ℚ, ℤ*, ... }` (`:195-196`); ℚ "is a subtype of ℝ" (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:36-37`).
- The types chapter of the same draft says the opposite: "Moreover, there are several simple standard numeric types. These types are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them." (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex:500-502`, the list that follows names ℤ, ℕ, ℚ, ℝ, ℂ and every fixed width). That sentence is not in the text of the 2008 release (searched) and is in the draft by February 2011; the cut history does not date it more closely. The 2012 Types chapter keeps it word for word (`types.tick:977-980`). So the draft contradicts itself, and the later text sides with exclusion.
- The compiler side went flat from the start. Chase, 2009-08-31: "ZZ32 is NOT a subtype of ZZ64, RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64; this would be a good time to get coercion working" (`6896886fb`). Maessen, 2009-11-17: "expect more coercions to come on line as we gradually migrate to a flat numeric hierarchy" (`128f313b5`). Steele added the prelude's `Comparison` traits with their `extends` clauses commented out on 2011-07-15 (`b3c2e1342`) and had `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` as siblings under `Number` by 2011-07-22 (`da5291587`). Steele's 2016 slide draws `Number → {Integral → ZZ32, ZZ64, ZZ; Float → RR32, RR64}` (`SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md:159-161`).
- Rounding: the draft's rational chapter declares `floor`, `⌊⌋`, `ceiling`, `⌈⌉`, `round`, `truncate` all returning ℤ, and says `round` sends an exact half to the even integer (`basic-lib/numbers.tex:457-472`). It has no chapter for the floating-point types. The 2008 release, in its library listing, declares for floats what C and IEEE do: `floor(a: Number): RR64`, `⌊a⌋: ZZ64`, `ceiling(a: Number): RR64`, `⌈a⌉: ZZ64`, `truncate(a: Number): ZZ64` (the 1.0 PDF, pdftotext lines 8295-8299). The interpreter's api declares the same on `RR64`: `floor(self): RR64`, `|\self/| : ZZ64`, `ceiling(self): RR64`, `|/self\| : ZZ64`, `truncate(self): ZZ64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:368-372`); its component body is inconsistent with the api (`|\self/| : ZZ`, `truncate(self): RR64`, `round(self): ZZ`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:470-475`). The team's prelude declared none of them for `RR64` and left `floor(self): RR64` and `ceiling(self): RR64` in a comment (`git show 5a68404fd:ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi`, lines 438-439).
- Overflow: "For integer results, overflow throws an `IntegerOverflow`" (`basic/operators/opr-overview.tex:154-155`, `:195-196`), kept by Steele in the 2012 restart; wrapping has its own operators ∔ ∸ ⨰ and saturation ⊞ ⊟ ⊡ (`:172-176`, `:205-209`). The interpreter wrapped silently; Maessen's 2007 comment calls the range checks not yet done.
- Where they left it open: how to have both the exclusion rule (below) and ℤ inside ℚ. Naden, 2012: the numeric hierarchy is written with the self-type idiom, it has "crossed instantiations of the kind that we determined must be outlawed", the self-type bound fixes one failure and not the other, "Victor and John have started working on this sort of theory with their trolls", and "more work needs to be done in order to understand how to best support the numerical hierarchy in the Fortress type system" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:568-632`). Nobody solved it.

### Generics and their specialisation

- A **static parameter** is a parameter of a declaration filled at compile time or at run time: a type (`List[\T\]`), a number (`Vector[\T, nat n\]`), a boolean, an operator, a dimension. An **instantiation** fills it (`List[\ZZ\]`). Fortress **reifies** generics: a value carries its instantiation at run time, so dispatch can tell `List[\Boolean\]` from `List[\String\]` (Steele 2016, slide 41). Java erases them; this is where Fortress departed from Java.
- **Specialisation** is a generic declaration beside a special version for one instantiation: `tail[\X\](x: List[\X\])` beside `tail(x: List[\ZZ\])`, chosen at run time by the value. Naden's 2011 workshop paper says the library's authors "found it useful ... to define both monomorphic and polymorphic versions of functions" (`reviews/mie-probes/literature.md` § 1). The team's tests and the checker's dispatcher are built for it.
- To make that sound they adopted **multiple instantiation exclusion**: no type may be a subtype of two different instantiations of one generic ("a rule that forbids multiple instantiation inheritance, in which a type (other than Bottom) is a subtype of distinct applications of a type constructor", `Papers/Types/exclusion.tick:141-152`; in the checker since 2010-05-28 and as `checkP` since 2010-07-26). The 2012 Types chapter renames it "instantiation exclusion" and adds a `covariant` modifier (`types.tick:322-339`, `:353-372`). Naden: "Fortress implements blanket multiple instantiation exclusion for the semantic benefits and the simplicity of the restriction" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:496-497`). The tower breaks it because each level says "I am `Equality` at my own type", so one `ZZ32` is `Equality` at five instantiations.
- **Run-time instantiation**: when dispatch picks a generic declaration the static call did not select, its parameters must be inferred at run time; the 2011 paper says so and leaves how "beyond the scope of this paper" (`Papers/Types/rules.tick:118-129`). Welterweight aims for "the most specific instantiation of an applicable entrypoint" (`Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:67`). Steele's 2016 slide 44, "Where We Got Stuck": generic methods with symmetric dispatch need the parametric meet rule and the return-type rule, which need "nontrivial run-time constraint solving" ("a euphemism for exponential cost"); "So we had a grand vision, but could not quite pull it off." Naden's last memo (`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/`) restricts the instance by the static return type; implemented on neither path.
- **`where` clauses**, a second way to bind a type variable ("Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves", `basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-352`, and `object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}`, `:384-397`): "Widening and where clauses are not yet supported" (`basic/conversions-coercions.tex:15`); code generation refuses any declaration with one (FACTS:158).

### Overloading and dispatch

- Fortress has **symmetric multimethods**: an overloaded call is resolved on all its arguments, once statically (the most specific declaration applicable to the static types) and again at run time (the most specific applicable to the run-time types, `basic/overloading.tex:262-276`). The **return-type rule** ties the two: a more specific declaration's result must fit the less specific one's, so the run-time choice never returns something the static choice did not promise.
- On static parameters the 2008 release had a first model that "may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine are implemented" (the 1.0 PDF, lines 5234-5241). The 2009 draft replaced it with a ban: "it is an error for their static parameters to differ ... Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which declarations are applicable" (`basic/overloading.tex:100-107`), and in the same draft listed "Relaxing restrictions on static parameters of overloaded functionals" as future work with Jan Maessen's `array1` pair (`appendices/future.tex:236-266`). The 2011 paper allows differing static parameters under three rules (No Duplicates, Meet, Return Type), the checker enforces them, walk never enforced the ban, and the 2012 restart drops the sentence.

### Coercion

- A **coercion** is a conversion a trait declares from another type (`trait ZZ64 ... coerce(z: ZZ32)`), inserted by the compiler where no declaration applies without it. It is not chained (`conversions-coercions.tex:127-130`). "For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a declaration that is applicable without coercion. If so, the most specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are explicitly added" (`:454-462`). It is resolved on static types: "Notice that coercion is resolved statically", with an example where `c: C = D` and `f(c)` calls `f(A)` by coercion "despite the fact that the declaration f(B) is applicable to the dynamic call f(D)" (`:598-635`). The draft's own example of widths declares `ZZ64 coerce(z: ZZ32)` and `ZZ128` from both (`:549-565`); no sentence makes `ZZ32` a subtype of `ZZ64`. "Fortress supports the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point values" (`:64-66`), a general sentence.
- Numerals: "numerals have their own types ... This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-148`); the types named (`NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`) carry the value and were never implemented; a note says "We need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy" (`:83-95`). The prelude has one `IntLiteral`, a sibling each number type coerces from (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390-429`; Maessen 2009: "ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec"). The interpreter's is `object IntLiteral extends { ZZ32 }` with its arithmetic commented out: "Do not enable these until coercion is implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals." (`FortressBuiltin.fss:497-498`).
- The prelude's coercions are every exact integer pair and none from an integer into a float (`reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md` § 5, checked at `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:103-108`, `:147-149`, `:433-435`).

### Sizes

- A **`nat` parameter** is a static parameter that is a number: `Vector[\T, nat n\]`. "These parameters are instantiated at runtime with numeric values. A nat parameter may be used ... to appear in any context that a variable of type ℕ32 can appear" (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:78-90`). The library's arrays and matrices carry their sizes this way and their products require the inner sizes to agree (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1680-1684`). The team's checker never checked them ("Todo: Handle int, nat, bool args"), the code generator reserved a slot for them (`CodeGen.java:5317-5328`), and the library's `NatReflect.fss:38-40` says of making a size from a run-time number "Really this just proves that it can be done without extending the language. Having proven that, we ought to build it in".
- Unboxing (storing a float as a machine double, not as an object) was intended and never built: `compiler/optimization/Unbox.java:12-19` and the loader's empty "expando" stub (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:168-172`).

### `comprises` and exclusion

- **`excludes`** declares that two traits share no value; an object type excludes every type not above it (`basic/types-vals-vars.tex:212-224`). Exclusion is what lets the checker prove two overloads never both apply.
- **`comprises`** closes a trait: `trait Number comprises { RR64, QQ, AnyIntegral }` lists the types below it. The draft reads the list at the level of types: the listed traits "are exactly the traits that immediately extend T" (`basic/traits.tex:231-234`, a draft note). The 2012 texts read it at the level of values: an instantiation "is covered by the union of the types in this set" (`types.tick:384-389`); "no value can belong to the trait unless it also belongs to one of the comprised types" (`Papers/Welterweight/grammar.tick:21-22`). The draft's future-work list says "We agreed to revise the Meet rule to address this with the coverage check" (`appendices/future.tex:285`).
- The **self-type idiom**: `trait Ring[\X\] comprises X`, so `Ring[\ℚ\]` "is really just ℚ itself" (Naden, `:576-582`); the patents of 2012-08-31 make it a named exception to the exclusion rule ("Self-types meet"), never built.

### The libraries

- The specification knows one library, "chiefly `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/library/structure.tex:15-18`). The compiler prelude was cut on 2008-12-19 as a "Hopefully temporary hack as we work on importing java objects cleanly" (`WellKnownNames.java:110-111`) and grown for three and a half years; the team called what went into it "bogus" (2009).
- The library's own flavour: algebra traits (`AdditiveGroup[\T\]`, `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`, `StandardTotalOrder[\T\]`), each self-typed, carried by every number type; reductions licensed by associativity and identity; open marker traits (`AnyMaybe`, `AnyList`) with a "not yet" comment where a `where`-clause `comprises` was wanted (`FortressLibrary.fsi:434`). The specified algebraic-constraints library (monoids, groups, rings, fields, `HasIdentity`) exists only commented out (`Library/incomplete/`). Steele's 2016 slide 12 promised "Rational, complex, and quaternion"; only rational shipped.

### Where the designers left the question open, in one list

- Both the exclusion rule and the nested tower (Naden's "more work needs to be done").
- Run-time instantiation of a dispatched generic (the 2011 paper's "beyond the scope"; Naden's unfinished memo).
- Inference of static arguments at a call (`basic/inference.tex` is a 27-line stub).
- A numeral's type hierarchy ("We need to describe").
- The float types' rounding methods (no chapter; three inconsistent spellings in their own library).
- Whether `comprises` is read on types or on values (two readings, the later one on values).
- `where` clauses and widening (never supported).
- Sizes in the checker and at run time (a "Todo", a reserved slot, "we ought to build it in").
- Which integer width a range has (no sentence; the prelude says `ZZ32`).

## 2. The decisions, one by one

Three verdicts are used. **Faithful**: the designers' latest word says this. **A call**: the designers left no word; consistent or not with his principles. **A departure**: against the designers' latest word; justified or not. For anything judged wrong: what it has cost, and what reversing it costs now.

### F1. The goal and its measuring stick (2026-09-16)

- Verdict: a call, and the right frame. Two corrections to its wording. "The July 2012 draft" names the right tree and the wrong date: the team's text is of 2010-12, and it is now revised in place, so "judged by `Specification/`" reads partly the revival's own words (25 revision sections, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`). Answer 1 (2026-09-26) got the citation right, "the Working Draft of February 2011"; the goal's sentence in CLAUDE.md and POSITIONS:24 has not caught up.
- Citation: `coordinator/spec-lineage.md` §§ 2, 4; FACTS:143.
- Cost: none in the work; a reader is misled about when the text was written. Fix: one sentence.

### F2. The library's own practice is the standard (2026-09-19)

- Verdict: a call, consistent with principle 1 ("custodians, not authors"). It is also the ground on which two of his decisions should have been made and were not (D6's row 330, D23's decision 2). Where it pulls against route A (the practice was the nesting), his yes of 2026-09-24 settled that the practice is the library's patterns, not every one of its shapes.

### F3. The later, implementation-informed word outweighs the early text (2026-09-23, 2026-09-26)

- Verdict: a call, and the right one for this language, whose draft says one thing in its types chapter and another in its library chapters. Its limit, which the exclusion brief named: it ranks texts by date and by whether they ran, and the two implemented halves (the interpreter's nested library, the compiler's flat prelude and rule) are both the group's. Where it leaves a judgement he made one (D4).
- Citation: `reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md:127-131`.

### D1. One library, the interpreter's (2026-09-20, 09-21)

- Verdict: faithful. The specification names one library; the split's own comment calls it a temporary hack; nothing on record argues for two as a destination.
- Citation: `library/structure.tex:15-18`; `WellKnownNames.java:110-111`; `coordinator/library-route-judgement.md` § 1.
- Cost: the price is the route itself. Every checker error on the interpreter's library became path work: 1.7K errors on 2026-09-27, 627 now (FACTS:56). The part not yet designed is the destination's last step, the switch-over (section 3, O1).

### D2. Sizes in the types and unboxed `double[]`, together (2026-09-19); row 40 closed with no decision (2026-09-25)

- Verdict: faithful to the design, which put sizes in types and intended unboxing, and never built either on the compiled path. Closing row 40 as "no decision taken" was right: the worker's three defaults were refuted by probe.
- Citation: `basic/trait-parameters.tex:82`; `Unbox.java:12-19`; `NatReflect.fss:38-40`; `reviews/array-design-review.md:13-37`.
- What it will cost him: the array review's first finding stands. The model's arrays are unsized in its own types, so on the compiled path "the model's text is the notation" and "sizes are central" collide on every operator application. Decision D's diff measures the collision: 21 model lines out, 29 in, no operator changed, 24 own errors to 12 (`reviews/decision-d-diff.md` § 1), and it is stale since `tabulate`. This is his decision to take with the diff in front of him, not a repair (section 6, item 6).

### D3. The scalar-extension block, `AnyAdditiveGroup`, `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ }` (2026-09-21)

- Verdict: a call, approved as landed; the closure was held until measured, which was right. The block is the revival's invention argued from `Number` membership rather than from the algebra the library gives arithmetic (Astra's point; `reviews/batch-6-conformance.md:90`). It blocked the library's own open-marker way when `AnyIntegral` came back (D24). Not wrong; a reminder that phase 5's array bodies need capability bounds, not `Number`.
- Citation: `reviews/library-scalar-extension-review.md`; `reviews/anyintegral-comprises-judgement.md` § 2, way 1.

### D4. Route A: keep the rule, flatten the tower, teach walk coercion (2026-09-24)

- Verdict: faithful to the designers' latest implemented word, and justified. This is the decision the evidence author asked to be looked at hardest, so the reasoning in full:
  - For the rule: it is the group's implemented and published position (2010 checker, 2011 paper, 2012 Types chapter, Naden's "blanket" sentence, POPL 2019).
  - For the flat tower: the compiler side chose it in 2009 (Chase, Maessen) and built it in 2011 (Steele); the draft's own types chapter says the numeric types are "mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them", and the 2012 Types chapter repeats it; Steele's 2016 slide draws it flat; every high-performance peer he named (Julia, Swift, Rust, X10) is flat with explicit or coerced widening.
  - Against: the library chapters' prose and the interpreter's library, both 2008, never checked; Naden's aim to keep both, which he left unsolved; the patents' forest rule, never built, whose soundness rule the revival would have had to write itself (route C, built as a shadow: 188 lines in 5 files, a return-type rule of ours, the interpreter overflowing on `comprises T`, FACTS:48).
  - On "the mutually exclusive sentence": the route-A notes cite ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ as what the specification states and do not cite this sentence (`reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md:39`; the flattening note cites both, `reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md:181`, `:454`). Had the brief cited it, his case would have been stronger, not weaker: the specification's types chapter, the later of its two voices, already said what route A does. The revised number chapters now agree with it (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, the `revival-rationals` callout).
  - On Naden's unsolved aim: route A does not solve it; it gives it up, keeping the rule and letting ℤ reach ℚ and ℝ64 by coercion. That is what Naden's own self-type-bound rewrite points to ("a flat tower's idiom", the brief § 4), and what his principle of 2026-09-29 accepts: an unfinished corner accepted to get to one program.
- Citation: `types-vals-vars.tex:500-502`; `types.tick:977-980`; `6896886fb`; `128f313b5`; `b3c2e1342`; `da5291587`; `justificationOfRTR.tex:496-497`, `:630-632`.
- What it has cost: `Number` lost its catch-alls, so `Number`'s `=` is not transitive (row 434); 89 team test lines respelled; 21 of the team's 24 demos with an unwritten clause-form sum fail and are not gated (`reviews/batch-6-conformance.md:75`); an integer scalar meeting a float array was refused under walk until batch N; and the interpreter chooses coercions on run-time values (D4's second half, judged under tension 5 below). Reversal to C: FACTS:48's price plus everything built on the flat tower since batch 6.

### D5. Design B for a size at run time, with the factory (2026-09-24, 09-26)

- Verdict: a call in a gap the team left ("Non-type args will be somewhat problematic at first", `OverloadSet.java:1213`), filling the slot the team's code generator reserved, with the team's own factory pattern. Consistent.
- Citation: `CodeGen.java:5317-5328`; `InstantiatingClassloader.java:2744-2752`; FACTS:114.

### D6. Rows 329 and 330: rounding (2026-09-21)

- Row 329, half to even on floats: faithful to the rational rule, Steele's own ℚ body and IEEE's default; the history found no reason for the float `round`'s half-up. Right.
- Row 330, `floor`, `ceiling`, `round`, `truncate` and the brackets returning unbounded ℤ on the float types: **a departure, not justified as it stands.**
  - The designers' word on floats is consistent across the 2008 release (`floor(a: Number): RR64`, `⌊a⌋: ZZ64`, `ceiling: RR64`, `⌈⌉: ZZ64`, `truncate: ZZ64`) and the interpreter's api (`FortressLibrary.fsi:368-372`, the same five). Only the component body and the prelude's comment are inconsistent, and they are inconsistent among ZZ, ZZ64 and RR64 for the brackets and `truncate`, never for the named `floor` and `ceiling`, which return the float in every text the team wrote. The rational chapter's "all ℤ" rule is stated of ℚ. The 2008 listing was not on the table when he decided; the ledger row and the coordinator's ask cite the api and the prelude only.
  - His stated reason, "ℤ sits under ℚ under ℝ64 in the tower, so an integer result goes back into float arithmetic by promotion", no longer holds: under route A and answer 8, ℤ reaches ℝ64 only by an explicit `asFloat` (row 330's last note; FACTS:116). So `floor(x) + y` with `y: RR64` would not type-check; a program writes `asFloat(floor(x))`. 1	Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance
2	
3	GYUNGHEE PARK, KAIST, South Korea and Oracle Labs, USA
4	JAEMIN HONG, KAIST, South Korea
5	GUY L. STEELE JR., Oracle Labs, USA
6	SUKYOUNG RYU, KAIST, South Korea
7	Many object-oriented languages provide method overloading, which allows multiple method declarations with
8	the same name. For a given method invocation, in order to choose what method declaration to invoke, multiple
9	dispatch considers the run-time types of the arguments. While multiple dispatch can support binary methods
10	(such as mathematical operators) intuitively and consistently, it is difficult to guarantee that calls will be
11	neither ambiguous nor undefined at run time, especially in the presence of expressive language features such
12	as multiple inheritance and parametric polymorphism. Previous efforts have formalized languages that include                   11
13	such features by using overloading rules that guarantee a unique and type-sound resolution of each overloaded
14	method call; in many cases, such rules resolve ambiguity by treating the arguments asymmetrically. Here we
15	present the first formal specification of a strongly typed object-oriented language with symmetric multiple
16	dispatch, multiple inheritance, and parametric polymorphism with variance. We define both a static (type-
17	checking) semantics and a dynamic (dispatching) semantics and prove the type soundness of the language,
18	thus demonstrating that our novel dynamic dispatch algorithm is consistent with the static semantics. Details
19	of our dynamic dispatch algorithm address certain technical challenges that arise from structural asymmetries
20	inherent in object-oriented languages (e.g., classes typically declare ancestors explicitly but not descendants).
21	CCS Concepts: · Software and its engineering → General programming languages; · Social and pro-
22	fessional topics → History of programming languages;
23	Additional Key Words and Phrases: Method Overloading, Symmetric Multiple Dispatch, Parametric Polymor-
24	phism, Variance
25	ACM Reference Format:
26	Gyunghee Park, Jaemin Hong, Guy L. Steele Jr., and Sukyoung Ryu. 2019. Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple
27	Dispatch with Variance. Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 3, POPL, Article 11 (January 2019), 28 pages. https:

30	1 INTRODUCTION
31	In object-oriented languages, method overloading and its unique resolution are important features.
32	Method overloading allows multiple method declarations of the same name but different parameter
33	types. Thus, it enables to define different behaviors of + or equal for different parameter types,
34	for example. For a given overloaded method invocation of equal, a resolution mechanism should
35	select a single declaration to call among the overloaded declarations of equal using the argument
36	types of the method invocation.
37	   When resolving an overloaded method invocation, dynamic dispatch considers the run-time types
38	of the arguments of the method invocation. When a dispatch mechanism considers the run-time

56	type of only a single argument, usually the receiver of a method call, as in languages like C++ and
57	Java, it is single dispatch. By contrast, multiple dispatch considers the run-time types of more than
58	one argument as in languages like Common Lisp, Fortress, and Julia. Especially, symmetric multiple
59	dispatch considers multiple arguments equally, which supports mathematical operators like binary
60	methods intuitively and uniformly [Clifton et al. 2000].
61	   While method overloading and its resolution by dynamic dispatch give a consistency in naming
62	methods that logically perform very similar tasks, they impose two restrictions to guarantee a
63	unique and type-sound resolution of each overloaded method invocation [Castagna et al. 1992, 1995].
64	First, the dispatch mechanism should be able to find the most specific applicable method declaration
65	for any overloaded method invocation. A method declaration is applicable to given arguments if its
66	parameter types are supertypes of the types of the arguments. One method declaration is more
67	specific than another if the domain type of the former is a subtype of that of the latter. Hereafter,
68	we consider that every method declaration has a single parameter possibly a tuple of two or more
69	components, and call the parameter type of a method declaration its domain type. Second, for
70	a given overloaded method invocation, its static type should be a supertype of the return type
71	of a dynamically chosen method declaration by the dispatch mechanism. Otherwise, a method
72	invocation result may be used in a type-unsound manner.
73	   Moreover, expressive language features often add various possibilities to make overloaded method
74	invocations ambiguous. As we discuss below, such features make it difficult to design a language
75	that guarantees no ambiguous nor undefined calls at run time.
76	   One such a feature is multiple inheritance, which allows one class to extend multiple classes. While
77	multiple inheritance supports modular and reusable code, it easily introduces ambiguous method
78	calls. Because one parent class may not be more specific than another parent class, dynamically
79	selecting the most specific applicable method declaration may be unclear. For example, consider
80	that each of two classes A and B has a method declaration m with the same parameter type Number,
81	class C extends both A and B, and c is an instance of C. Then, evaluation of c.m(0) results in an
82	ambiguous call because neither A nor B is more specific than each other.
83	   Another feature is parametric polymorphism, or generics. By introducing type parameters in
84	class and method declarations, parametric polymorphism enables programmers to manage types
85	in a fine-grained way. For example, the List class may be instantiated as either ListJStringK or
86	ListJIntegerK. However, selecting the most specific applicable declaration among polymorphic
87	method declarations at run time is not trivial. Moreover, many languages with parametric polymor-
88	phism support automatic inference for the type arguments of polymorphic method invocations; at
89	run time, dynamic dispatch must not only find the most specific applicable declaration, but also
90	infer appropriate type arguments for that declaration.
91	   Finally, variance defines additional subtype relations for polymorphic types [Igarashi and Viroli
92	2006]. Without variance, instances of the same polymorphic type are in a subtype relation only
93	when their type arguments are the same type. Variance supports subtype relationships between
94	different instances of the same polymorphic type by allowing the programmer to label each type
95	parameter of a class covariant, contravariant, or invariant. If a parametric type T has one covariant
96	type parameter, then it preserves the subtype relation of its type argument; hence, when a type
97	P is a subtype of another type Q, which we write P <: Q, it implies T JP K <: T JQ K. If the type
98	parameter of T is contravariant, then T reverses the subtype relationship of its type arguments;
99	hence, P <: Q implies T JQ K <: T JP K. If the type parameter of T is invariant, then T JP K <: T JQ K
100	only if P ≡ Q, where P ≡ Q denotes that P and Q are equivalent, that is, P is a subtype of Q and vice
101	versa. Variance annotations allow the programmer to define more expressive polymorphic methods.
102	For example, consider the following excerpt from the List class source code in Scala [EPFL 2017]:
103	
104

109	                ···
110	                def :::[B >: A](prefix: List[B]): List[B] = · · ·
111	                ···

113	The List class takes a single covariant (denoted by +) type parameter A, and the ::: method
114	concatenates two lists, its receiver and argument. If A were invariant, the element type B of the
115	argument list should be a supertype of the element type A of the receiver list. However, since A
116	is covariant, the method can take a list of any element type C that is less than or equal to B, and
117	return a list whose element type is B, which is a common supertype of the element types of its
118	receiver and argument: A<:B and C<:B. As one might expect, variance also increases the difficulty
119	of overloading resolution.
120	   Therefore, supporting symmetric multiple dispatch in the presence of various expressive language
121	features has been a long-standing effort. Previous efforts have formalized a variety of core calculi
122	that capture some of the aforementioned features in a piecemeal rather than holistic fashion. While
123	they are widely different in terms of the expressivity, completeness, decidability, and correctness of
124	the formalization of the target languages and their type systems, they all define a set of overloading
125	rules that overloaded method declarations should satisfy to make dynamic dispatch select the most
126	specific applicable method declaration with a type-safe return type.
127	   For a simple object-oriented language with multiple inheritance, Allen et al. [2008, 2007] and
128	Kim and Ryu [2011] presented three overloading rules: Exclusion Rule, Subtype Rule, and Meet
129	Rule. Every pair of method declarations with the same name must satisfy one of these overloading
130	rules. The authors proved that a set of overloaded method declarations satisfying the overloading
131	rules does not produce any ambiguous method invocation at run time.
132	   To understand the interplay between symmetric multiple dispatch and parametric polymorphism,
133	Allen et al. [2011] focused on a type system without any specific target language and informally
134	presented three other overloading rules: a No Duplicates Rule, a revised Meet Rule, and a Return
135	Type Rule, where every pair of method declarations with the same name must satisfy all three
136	overloading rules. The authors showed that interpreting a polymorphic method declaration as a set
137	of infinitely many monomorphic declarations is not appropriate for overloading resolution. Instead,
138	they considered a polymorphic method declaration as a single declaration whose domain type is
139	existentially quantified over its type parameters as proposed by Bourdoncle and Merz [1997].
140	   In this paper, we present a formal core calculus FGFV (Featherweight Generic Fortress with Vari-
141	ance) for an object-oriented language with symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple inheritance, and
142	parametric polymorphism with variance. For conciseness, FGFV omits functional methods [Allen
143	et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to
144	FGFV in an obvious way. Unlike the prior work, we formally present overloading rules for FGFV,
145	define its dynamic semantics with a novel dynamic dispatch algorithm, and prove type soundness.
146	As we discuss in Section 5.4, defining a provable system for an object-oriented language with
147	asymmetric features requires careful tradeoffs between static expressivity and dynamic efficiency.
148	   In the rest of the paper, we first describe the previous efforts in more detail with concrete
149	code examples (Section 2). After presenting the FGFV calculus that represents an object-oriented
150	language with symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple inheritance, parametric polymorphism, and
151	variance (Section 3), we formally define the overloading rules for FGFV (Section 4). Then, we define
152	both static and dynamic overloading resolution with a novel dynamic dispatch algorithm, and
153	sketch proofs of the type soundness of FGFV (Section 5). Full proofs are available in a companion
154	report [Park et al. 2018]. Finally, we discuss related work (Section 6) and conclude (Section 7).

161	2 MOTIVATION
162	In this section, we first discuss existing research achievements in the pursuit of formally defining
163	object-oriented languages with symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple inheritance, and parametric
164	polymorphism with variance. Then, we present how FGFV completes the long-standing endeavor
165	by defining a core calculus with static overloading rules and a dynamic dispatch algorithm that are
166	proven type-sound.

168	2.1 Overloading Rules for Multiple Inheritance
169	As we discussed in Section 1, both symmetric multiple dispatch and multiple inheritance may cause
170	ambiguous method calls that cannot be resolved at run time. Let us assume that class C is the only
171	subtype of both classes A and B, and they are all distinct throughout this section. Consider the
172	following overloaded method declarations of m 1 :
173	                    m 1 (x: B, y: C): B = · · ·               m 1 (x: C, y: B): B = · · ·
174	which have the same return type B but different domain types (B, C) and (C, B). For a method
175	invocation m 1 (c, c) where the run-time type of c is C, it is ambiguous which declaration to invoke
176	due to symmetric multiple dispatch: both method declarations are applicable to (c, c) since both
177	(B, C) and (C, B) are supertypes of (C, C), and neither declaration is more specific than the other.
178	Also, consider the following overloaded declarations of m 2 :
179	                    m 2 (x: A):Boolean = · · ·                m 2 (x: B):Boolean = · · ·
180	which have domain types A and B, respectively. For a method invocation m 2 (c), it is ambiguous
181	which declaration to invoke due to multiple inheritance: both declarations are applicable to c and
182	neither declaration is more specific than the other.
183	   In order to guarantee that no such ambiguous method calls are possible at run time, researchers
184	have proposed several calculi with restrictions on overloaded method declarations. CF [Allen et al.
185	2007], Core Fortress, is a core calculus of the Fortress programming language [Allen et al. 2008],
186	which contains components, top-level functions, functional methods, and declarations of exclusive
187	types in addition to multiple inheritance. However, it does not specify the language semantics and
188	informally provides rules for valid overloaded method declarations. FFMM [Kim and Ryu 2011],
189	Featherweight Fortress with Multiple Dispatch and Multiple Inheritance, simplified CF to focus only
190	on multiple inheritance, and it has a complete formalization of the language semantics including
191	overloading rules and its type soundness proof in Coq. Since the overloading rules of CF and FFMM
192	are the same, we will refer to these two languages collectively as Featherweight Fortress (FF).
193	   The overloading rules of FF require every pair in a set of overloaded method declarations to
194	satisfy one of the following rules:
195	    Exclusion Rule: Their domain types are exclusive (their intersection is Bottom, where the
196	       Bottom type is a subtype of every type and no value belongs to Bottom).
197	    Subtype Rule: The domain type of one declaration is a strict subtype of the domain type of
198	       the other, and the return type of the former is a subtype of the return type of the latter.
199	    Meet Rule: The domain types are not exclusive nor in a subtype relation, and the overloaded
200	       set contains a third disambiguating method declaration which we call the meet of the pair.
201	       The meet of two method declarations is more specific than each of the declarations and less
202	       specific than any other method declaration that is more specific than both declarations.
203	   Let us revisit the previous examples, with an additional method declaration each for m 1 and m 2 :

601	The overloading rules require that every pair in a set of overloaded method declarations satisfies all
602	three rules defined in Figure 5. To determine whether one method declaration is more specific than
603	the other, while the informal rules in Section 2.2 used the subset relation of their applicable sets,
604	which is not practically checkable, we use the subtype relation of their domain types as in Allen
605	et al. [2011]. Note that even though FGFV additionally supports variance annotations of trait type
606	parameters, the overloading rules for FGF remain the same because covariant or contravariant types

609	Triv], [Meet-Triv], and [Return-Triv]). The No Duplicates Rule also checks whether the domain
610	types of two declarations are different; if the domain type of one declaration is not a subtype of the
611	domain type of the other, they satisfy the rule ([No-Dup-Not-Less] and [No-Dup-Not-Gtr]). The
612	Meet Rule is satisfied if two domain types exclude each other ([Meet-Excl]), they are in a subtype
613	relation ([Meet-Less] and [Meet-Gtr]), or the domain type of a third declaration of the same

1221	5.4     Discussion
1222	Defining a provable system for an object-oriented language requires addressing various technical
1223	challenges due to the structural asymmetries inherent in the language design. One can have a
1224	variable of type Any, but one cannot have a variable of type Bottom. The ilk of an actual argument
1225	must be a subtype, not a supertype, of the method’s parameter type. The ilk of a returned value
1226	must be a subtype, not a supertype, of the method’s return type. A trait may declare ancestors but
1227	not descendants. Such asymmetries prohibit seemingly symmetric features from being treated as
1228	duals. One might think at first glance that upper bounds and lower bounds of type parameters
1229	should be related symmetrically (perhaps treated as duals), but they cannot be.
1230	   For example, the łAncestor Meet Rulež (expressed in this paper by rule [Anc-Same-Trait]) was
1231	introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase [Steele and Chase 2012] to design
1232	an expressive type system with union and intersection types. This rule permits proofs that (a) if
1233	T JP K is covariant in P then T J(α ⊓ α ′)K ≡ (T Jα K ⊓ T Jα ′ K), and (b) if T JP K is contravariant in P
1234	then T J(α ⊔ α ′)K ≡ (T Jα K ⊓ T Jα ′ K) (that last set operator is indeed ⊓, not ⊔). These equivalences
1235	allow simplification of type expressions by moving type union and type intersection operators
1236	out of type arguments. However, the łobvious other two casesž are not available. When T JP K is
1237	covariant in P, T J(α ⊔ α ′)K is not equivalent to some simple combination of T Jα K and T Jα ′ K; the
1238	best one can say is that (T Jα K ⊔ T Jα ′ K) <: T J(α ⊔ α ′)K.
1239	   In 2012, the developers of Fortress explored an alternate set of language restrictions that exploited
1240	these asymmetries to ensure that exponential blowup could occur at run time only when union
1241	types interacted with contravariance (the dual case of intersection types interacting with covariance
1242	could not occur). They then contemplated two alternatives for avoiding the exponential blowup.
1243	One possibility is to eliminate contravariant type parameters and contravariant type relationships.
1244	This has the consequence that arrow types must be treated as invariant, rather than contravariant,
1245	in the type to the left of the arrow. This could make it inconvenient to use higher-order functions
1246	such as map, but one can compensate by introducing rules of coercion, so that if a function of type
1247	(α → ρ) is used in a situation where a function of type (α ′ → ρ ′) is required, it can be coerced to a
1248	new function object if α ′ <: α and ρ <: ρ ′. The other possibility is to eliminate union types from the
1249	type theory; this might require restricting the language so that, for example, in an if-then-else
1250	expression, the type of the then subexpression must be either a supertype or a subtype of the else
1251	subexpression. Alternatively, some sort of pseudo-join (least common existing supertype) operation
1252	could be used. One could go even further, also eliminating intersection types from the type theory
1253	by further restricting the language and possibly using a pseudo-meet operation.
1254	   We carefully designed our dynamic dispatch algorithm to make a balanced tradeoff between static
1255	expressivity and dynamic efficiency. We accept the potential for exponential blowup because we
1256	believe that such cases are unlikely to arise in practice and the use of union and intersection types
1257	in the type theory, even if not directly expressible by the programmer, makes the language more
1258	expressive. Also, while one could in principle allow any lower bound to refer to any type parameter,
1259	dynamic overloading resolution would then have to solve a general set of type inequalities, requiring
1260	a complex technique with multiple iterations; we chose instead to impose left-to-right scoping
1261	on method type parameters, allowing use of a simple, one-pass right-to-left scan. We believe this
1262	tradeoff represents a relatively small sacrifice of expressivity for a large gain in dynamic efficiency.
1263	   Dynamically inferring type instantiations can incur run-time overhead. In simple invariant cases,
1264	we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero. For example, if we pass a value of type
1265	ListJStringK to a method such as fooJT K(x:ListJT K), T is matched only once and no union

1297	ensure type safety under symmetric multiple dispatch in an object-oriented language with multiple
1298	inheritance, and showed how to check the rules without requiring the entire type hierarchy. They
1299	proposed the overloading rules in the context of a set of class declarations and function declarations
1300	without defining a language with complete static and dynamic semantics. Therefore, their work
1301	does not guarantee that the static overloading rules and the way a language chooses a method to
1302	invoke at run time match correctly. While FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal
1303	exclusion, and closed types in their work, they can be added in an obvious way. As the related work
1304	section of Allen et al. [2011] discusses in detail, most earlier systems like Dubious [Millstein and
1305	Chambers 1999, 2002; Millstein 2003], MultiJava [Clifton et al. 2006], and F(EML) [Lee and Chambers
1306	2006] supported overloading with symmetric multiple dynamic dispatch with multiple inheritance,
1307	but without support for polymorphic methods or types. While ML ≤ [Bourdoncle and Merz 1997]
1308	integrates polymorphism and symmetric multiple dynamic dispatch, it lacks multiple inheritance.
1309	   ParaSail [Taft 2011, 2016] is a parallel programming language designed to support inherently safe
1310	and secure, highly parallel applications. It also constrains the scope of type parameters, prohibiting
1311	a bound on a type parameter from referring to type parameter bindings to its left, so that dynamic
1312	type inference can be fast. However, ParaSail does not support covariant and contravariant type
1313	parameters, and it does not provide any formal specification.
1314	   Julia [Bezanson et al. 2015, 2017] is a dynamic programming language with symmetric multiple
1315	dispatch. It provides a type declaration and type annotation sublanguage, but does not have a static
1316	type system. Thus, it does not check the validity of overloaded methods, and only uses the subtype
1317	relation to find the most specific method among overloaded methods at run time.
1318	
1319	                           Proc. ACM Program. Lang., Vol. 3, No. POPL, Article 11. Publication date: January 2019.
1320	 11:26                               Gyunghee Park, Jaemin Hong, Guy L. Steele Jr., and Sukyoung Ryu
1321	
1322	   Various languages provide different subsets of the FGFV features. Scala [Odersky et al. 2016]
1323	supports polymorphic types with variance, but it does not support symmetric multiple dispatch.
1324	FHJ [Wang et al. 2018] proposed a dispatch algorithm, which uses static types at run time to resolve
1325	overloading conflicts from unrelated methods that happen to have the same name and signature
1326	due to multiple inheritance. Castagna et al. [2015] presented a statically-typed calculus with
1327	dynamic (explicit) dispatch through pattern-matching, polymorphism, recursive types, semantic
1328	subtyping, and union, intersection, and negation type connectives. Their local type inference
1329	algorithm computes sets of type substitutions to insert in appropriate places in expressions. While
1330	their type-case expression and intersection type behave similarly to method overloading, they
1331	do not have a similar notion of overloading rules. Since the type-case expression executes the
1332	first matching expression, it does not introduce any ambiguity. For OCaml, Garrigue [2001; 2002]
1333	introduced a type inference system for structural polymorphism such as polymorphic records,
1334	polymorphic variants, and accurate matching. Type constraints are described by constraint domains
1335	that are defined separately from its type system, and the constraints contain some notion of lower
1336	and upper bounds, which respectively represent required and available labels or cases. He also
1337	extended his work with CoQ mechanization [Garrigue 2010, 2015]. The work of Castagna and
1338	Garrigue may serve as a possible starting point for finding the necessary substitution σ to satisfy
1339	the rule [E-Sub] for existential subtyping during static analysis. We believe that our work opens
1340	the gate to adding either variance annotation in the work of Castagna or a form of type-case in the
1341	work of Garrigue.
1342	
1343	7 CONCLUSION
1344	We defined FGFV, a core calculus for an object-oriented language with symmetric multiple dispatch,
1345	multiple inheritance, and parametric polymorphism with variance. In order to ensure type soundness
1346	of FGFV, it must guarantee no ambiguous method invocations at run time, and preserve type even
1347	when a method invocation is dispatched to a different method at run time from the method chosen
1348	at compile time. Thus, we formalized overloading rules using existential types and universal types
1349	quantified over method type parameters to mechanically check whether overloaded polymorphic
1350	methods are valid. As a result, in a well-formed program that satisfies the overloading rules, there
1351	always exists the single most specific method to invoke with respect to both static argument types
1352	and dynamic argument types. Further, with the static types of method invocation expressions
1353	delivered to run time, the dynamic semantics of FGFV that uses the new dynamic dispatch algorithm
1354	we presented is proven to make type-sound choices among applicable method declarations.

# The POPL 2019 paper against the judgement: what changes

## In short

- The paper confirms the large calls: the exclusion rule kept, the tower flat, the 2009 overload sentence gone, the three rules, the return-type rule in the form batch 7b's rung C plans, applicability and specificity on declared quantified domains, and the implicit bound `Any`.
- It contradicts one default and one mechanism, both in batches not yet run or cheap to change: item 30's "least instance" is the 2012 rule the paper says the team could not prove and abandoned; the checker's binding of an unconstrained type parameter to `Bottom` (rows 447, 425, 516) is what the paper's model forbids outright. The paper's rule for both is the same sentence: instantiate at the intersection of the upper bounds, the declared bound and the call's static return type, never at the value's type alone and never at `Bottom`.
- It adds four things the record lacked: that rule; the exact form of the overloading rules with "existential reduction"; a restriction that its proof needs (a method type parameter may not appear in another's upper bound), which the library's `SUM`, `BIG MAX` and `Integral` families break; and a phase-5 requirement, that the dispatcher must know the call's static return type at run time.
- Three things should be done differently, all cheap: item 30's sentence in 7b's rung S and one test pair in rung C; the `Bottom` binding replaced by the bound in one checker rung, which replaces the "treat as a throw" fix the judgement recommended for row 447; row 516's union replaced by the bound. Nothing on route A, answer 9, item 26 or the conversion order changes.

## 0. What the record knew, and what the paper says

The record's account (`literature.md` § 1) was right as far as it went: the paper keeps the invariant-instantiation exclusion through its ancestor rule, moves the return-type check to run time, and has no self types and no numeric tower. What it did not have, each checked in the text:

- The instance rule. "The Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique ... but we were unable to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of the upper bounds." (§ 5.4, p. 11:25, lines 1274-1284.) The rule itself is [Solve-Step] (§ 5.2.3, p. 11:19, lines 965-1016): the substitution for a parameter is the intersection of its computed upper bound and its declared upper bounds, checked against the lower bounds; "Because g' is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom."
- The static return type at run time. Dispatch "seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" ([R-Method], § 5.2.1, p. 11:17, lines 888-896); "the language semantics needs to make the static types of method invocations available at run time" (§ 2.3, p. 11:7, lines 329-331). The upper bound of a return-only parameter comes from that static return type ([Dispatch], line 875: `g match ρ - bounds`).
- The default bound. "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (§ 3.2, p. 11:9, lines 418-419). `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax" (line 438).
- The overloading rules in checkable form (§ 4, Figure 5, p. 11:13, lines 630-661): No Duplicates as non-subtyping of domains either way; Meet as exclusion, subtyping or a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to the intersection ([Meet-Third], line 645); Return Type as one universal subtyping check, `arrow(d1) ⊑ ∀[κ,κ']((α ⊓ α') → ρ')` ([Return-Test], lines 656-660). Specificity is subtyping of existentially quantified domains, "a sound approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets, [but] not complete" (§ 4.2, p. 11:13, lines 673-675), narrowed by "existential reduction", which collects the constraints that keep a domain off `Bottom` and solves them (lines 733-743, Figure 6).
- A restriction the proof needs. A method's type parameter bindings are well formed only if "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" and every reference falls within a left-to-right scope; "restriction (1) makes dynamic dispatch more efficient and restriction (2) makes it consistent" (§ 3.3, p. 11:11, lines 565-570); the one-pass right-to-left solve depends on it (lines 1010-1016, 1258-1262). Trait type parameters carry no such restriction.
- What the calculus leaves out. "FGFV omits functional methods [Allen et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way" (§ 1, p. 11:3, lines 142-144); "FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types in their work, [but] they can be added in an obvious way" (§ 6, p. 11:25, lines 1302-1303). No coercion, no `nat` parameters, no numbers.
- The exclusion rule's form and date. [Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11, lines 530-532): a class extending two instances of a trait must extend an instance below both; "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' ... was introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase" (§ 5.4, p. 11:24, lines 1230-1232). For an invariant parameter only the same instance is below both; for a covariant one the lower instance is.

- Cost. "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero"; for variant cases "caching or dynamic recompilation" (§ 5.4, pp. 11:24-25, lines 1263-1273).

There is no tower, no self type and no `comprises T` in it (searched).
- It adds one thing the route-C notes could not know: variance cannot rescue the tower. The self-typed algebra traits put their parameter in a parameter position (`opr =(self, other: T)`), and [D-Method] forbids a covariant parameter there (lines 571-572, 584-592). So `Equality[\+T\]` is ill formed, and the covariant clause of the ancestor rule, the only clause that admits two instances on one chain, is closed to the tower. The patents' forest rule stays what the record called it, a sketch outside the group's proven model.
- Nothing to do differently. One line for batch 7b's rung S: Appendix I's instantiation-exclusion entry cites [Anc-Same-Trait] beside the 2011 paper and the 2012 Types chapter.

# The POPL 2019 paper against the judgement: what changes

## In short

- The paper confirms the large calls: the exclusion rule kept, the tower flat, the 2009 overload sentence gone, the three rules, the return-type rule in the form batch 7b's rung C plans, applicability and specificity on declared quantified domains, and the implicit bound `Any`.
- It contradicts one default and one mechanism, both in batches not yet run or cheap to change: item 30's "least instance" is the 2012 rule the paper says the team could not prove and abandoned; the checker's binding of an unconstrained type parameter to `Bottom` (rows 447, 425, 516) is what the paper's model forbids outright. The paper's rule for both is the same sentence: instantiate at the intersection of the upper bounds, the declared bound and the call's static return type, never at the value's type alone and never at `Bottom`.
- It adds four things the record lacked: that rule; the exact form of the overloading rules with "existential reduction"; a restriction that its proof needs (a method type parameter may not appear in another's upper bound), which the library's `SUM`, `BIG MAX` and `Integral` families break; and a phase-5 requirement, that the dispatcher must know the call's static return type at run time.
- Three things should be done differently, all cheap: item 30's sentence in 7b's rung S and one test pair in rung C; the `Bottom` binding replaced by the bound in one checker rung, which replaces the "treat as a throw" fix the judgement recommended for row 447; row 516's union replaced by the bound. Nothing on route A, answer 9, item 26 or the conversion order changes.

## 0. What the record knew, and what the paper says

The record's account (`literature.md` § 1) was right as far as it went: the paper keeps the invariant-instantiation exclusion through its ancestor rule, moves the return-type check to run time, and has no self types and no numeric tower. What it did not have, each checked in the text:

- The instance rule. "The Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique ... but we were unable to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of the upper bounds." (§ 5.4, p. 11:25, lines 1274-1284.) The rule itself is [Solve-Step] (§ 5.2.3, p. 11:19, lines 965-1016): the substitution for a parameter is the intersection of its computed upper bound and its declared upper bounds, checked against the lower bounds; "Because g' is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom."
- The static return type at run time. Dispatch "seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" ([R-Method], § 5.2.1, p. 11:17, lines 888-896); "the language semantics needs to make the static types of method invocations available at run time" (§ 2.3, p. 11:7, lines 329-331). The upper bound of a return-only parameter comes from that static return type ([Dispatch], line 875: `g match ρ - bounds`).
- The default bound. "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (§ 3.2, p. 11:9, lines 418-419). `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax" (line 438).
- The overloading rules in checkable form (§ 4, Figure 5, p. 11:13, lines 630-661): No Duplicates as non-subtyping of domains either way; Meet as exclusion, subtyping or a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to the intersection ([Meet-Third], line 645); Return Type as one universal subtyping check, `arrow(d1) ⊑ ∀[κ,κ']((α ⊓ α') → ρ')` ([Return-Test], lines 656-660). Specificity is subtyping of existentially quantified domains, "a sound approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets, [but] not complete" (§ 4.2, p. 11:13, lines 673-675), narrowed by "existential reduction", which collects the constraints that keep a domain off `Bottom` and solves them (lines 733-743, Figure 6).
- A restriction the proof needs. A method's type parameter bindings are well formed only if "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" and every reference falls within a left-to-right scope; "restriction (1) makes dynamic dispatch more efficient and restriction (2) makes it consistent" (§ 3.3, p. 11:11, lines 565-570); the one-pass right-to-left solve depends on it (lines 1010-1016, 1258-1262). Trait type parameters carry no such restriction.
- What the calculus leaves out. "FGFV omits functional methods [Allen et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way" (§ 1, p. 11:3, lines 142-144); "FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types in their work, [but] they can be added in an obvious way" (§ 6, p. 11:25, lines 1302-1303). No coercion, no `nat` parameters, no numbers.
- The exclusion rule's form and date. [Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11, lines 530-532): a class extending two instances of a trait must extend an instance below both; "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' ... was introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase" (§ 5.4, p. 11:24, lines 1230-1232). For an invariant parameter only the same instance is below both; for a covariant one the lower instance is.
- Variance in full: marks `+ - =` on trait parameters, objects always invariant (§ 3.2, lines 406-409); a covariant parameter only in covariant positions, a contravariant one only in contravariant ones ([D-Method], § 3.3, pp. 11:11-12, lines 571-595); dispatch with variance marks (§ 5.2.2); exponential blowup only where union types meet contravariance, accepted (§ 5.4, lines 1239-1257); the two alternatives the team weighed in 2012, dropping contravariance or dropping union types.
- Cost. "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero"; for variant cases "caching or dynamic recompilation" (§ 5.4, pp. 11:24-25, lines 1263-1273).
